newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African export payment scheme ends on July 11.
newsitem.headline: S.African export payment scheme ends on July 11.

text.p: Budgetary constraints have prompted South Africa's department of trade and industry to announce the early termination of one of its most controversial export incentives from July 11.
"This decision now finally brings to an end an era of demand side subsidies," the department said in a statement on Wednesday.

The general export incentive scheme (GEIS) was introduced in 1990 to give local manufacturers a financial incentive to increase exports after years of isolation under apartheid. Payouts grew so much that they soon dominated the department's budget.
It also fell foul of GATT regulations because it was a direct subsidy to exporters.
GEIS has been gradually scaled down since 1994 and was due to be phased out completely by the end of 1997.

The department said that after a careful evaluation of claims, it realised it had the choice of either continuing with the present benefit of cash payments based on six percent of free-on-board (FOB) export values for a few months, or reducing the benefits to less than two percent for the rest of the year.
Reducing the benefit to two percent would be "neither a meaningful subsidy, nor would it be cost-effective to administer," the department said.
As a result, payments for claims between May 1 and July 11 would be paid out at six percent but after July 11, no payments would be made.

The department said that its budget for GEIS in 1997/98 had been cut by a nominal 33 percent to 1.05 billion rand of its total three billion rand budget. Payments at six percent to July 11 would be 1.06 billion rand, leaving a shortfall of 11 million rand.

The parliamentary trade and industry committee last week expressed concern that continued GEIS payments could divert valuable resources away from other, more suitable ways of making industry competitive.
It was also concerned about the open endedness of the scheme and the fact that qualifying firms had a right to payments whether or not enough funds had been budgeted.

The department said the emphasis would now be placed on so-called supply-side measures aimed at helping firms deal with the basic reasons for their uncompetitiveness through training programmes and technological support.

Although the move may come as a shock to firms which have not been restructuring ahead of it, many have said that GEIS had become almost worthless and had been offset by the depreciation of the rand, which made exports more competitive.
